title: Babies, Bathwater, and Grit
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Dave Stuart Jr. responds to a colleague's offhand dismissal of grit by arguing that educators should not discard a useful idea because it has been misused. He concedes that grit was peddled as a cure for poverty and sometimes reduced to compliance, but says rejecting it on those grounds is a lapse in clear thinking. He recommends Angela Duckworth's new book as a genuine addition to the literature, listing its new contributions such as effort counting twice, the nature and nurture of grit, and the value of quitting low-level goals. He ties the discussion to a single aim for teaching, the long-term flourishing of students, and notes that clear, compelling top-level goals make persistence easier. The warning throughout is against buzzwords and echoing favorite commentators instead of reading the source.
points: Misuse of grit, whether as poverty snake oil or as a classroom compliance slogan, does not invalidate the underlying research.
Clear thinking among educators does not happen by accident; it takes the work of reading and researching rather than following a favorite commenter.
Duckworth's book is presented as a real extension and clarification of her work, especially in how central passion is to her definition.
The author names long-term student flourishing as the single highest-order goal that makes persistence and passion sustainable.
Throwing out the baby with the bathwater is attributed to mindlessness, the failure to remember what is good once the bad is noticed.
quotes: I understand that the snake oil salesmen of education took grit and peddled it as a silver bullet for solving systemic poverty. I realize that in some schools grit became nothing more than “Sit down, shut up, and do your work.” I know that, harmfully, grit has been used to bolster arguments like “Poor people are poor because they don’t work hard enough.

The more I think about what it will take to improve long-term flourishing outcomes in US schools, the more I see that clear thinking is non-negotiable. We need as many clear thinking educators as possible, and in an age as such nobody thinks clearly by accident.
This is not another 10-minute TED Talk bloated up into a 50,000-word book. It is what books should be: significant additions to and clarifications of a body of work.

In the clarification sense, critics of grit can no longer say that Duckworth only pays lip service to passion; it’s an integral part of the book and its central concept. Without an understanding of what Duckworth means by passion, you can’t understand what she means by grit.

The reason I can’t stand buzzwordification is because buzzwords kill clear thinking, and according to another book I’ve been reading recently, “how teachers think really matters” [1]. So I’m not on a buzzword bandwagon here; I haven’t drank the grit Kool-Aid.

When we throw babies out with the bathwater the cause of the problem is mindlessness. We know the bathwater is bad, but we forget about what’s good. The misuses of grit have been bad, no doubt; we need to be wary about using them as an excuse not to think.
